clues: Any environmental, infectious, chemical, or physical agent capable of causing congenital anomalies or increasing their incidence.
Its impact depends on maternal-fetal genotype, dose, duration, and the developmental stage at exposure.
Embryos are maximally vulnerable to structural defects caused by these agents during weeks 3 through 8.
A structural abnormality of shape or position affecting a previously normally formed fetal body part.
It results from abnormal extrinsic mechanical molding forces, such as uterine constraint or severe oligohydramnios.
Congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) from intrauterine crowding is a classic example.
A morphological defect resulting from the extrinsic breakdown or interference with an originally normal developmental process.
It is typically caused by vascular accidents, ischemia, or mechanical strangulation.
Limb or digital amputation caused by amniotic bands is a classic example.

terms.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
clues: A severe congenital limb reduction malformation in which the long bones of the extremities are absent or markedly shortened.
Hands or feet are attached directly close to the trunk, resembling seal flippers.
It became infamous worldwide following maternal ingestion of thalidomide during weeks 4 to 5.

terms.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
clues: A potent oral retinoid medication prescribed for severe nodulocystic acne.
It disrupts cranial neural crest cell migration and HOX gene signaling when taken during early pregnancy.
It causes a characteristic embryopathy featuring microtia/anotia, cleft palate, thymic hypoplasia, and conotruncal heart defects.

terms.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
clues: The most severe end of a spectrum of developmental disorders caused by prenatal ethanol exposure.
It features pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, microcephaly, and neurobehavioral impairment.
Its hallmark craniofacial triad comprises short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, and a thin upper lip.

terms.sub: Drugs, Chemicals, and Maternal Factors as Teratogens
clues: A rare congenital spectrum characterized by incomplete development of the sacrum, coccyx, and lower lumbar vertebrae.
It is accompanied by lower-limb hypoplasia and neurogenic bladder or bowel dysfunction.
Poorly controlled maternal pregestational diabetes mellitus is its strongest known risk factor.
Multiple gestation resulting from the ovulation and fertilization of two separate oocytes by two distinct spermatozoa.
They are no more genetically similar than ordinary siblings born at different times and may be of opposite sexes.
They always develop with dichorionic, diamniotic fetal membranes.
A rare complication of monozygotic twinning occurring in roughly 1 in 50,000 to 100,000 births.
It results from incomplete division of the embryonic disc after day 13 post-fertilization.
They are classified anatomically by their site of fusion, such as thoracopagus or craniopagus.
A serious hemodynamic complication exclusive to monochorionic multiple gestations.
Unbalanced deep placental arteriovenous anastomoses shunt blood chronically from one fetus to the other.
The donor becomes anemic and oligohydramniotic, whereas the recipient develops polycythemia, polyhydramnios, and cardiac overload.
An oncofetal glycoprotein synthesized sequentially by the fetal yolk sac, gastrointestinal tract, and liver.
Its concentration in maternal serum rises markedly when a fetus has an open neural tube defect or gastroschisis.
Conversely, second-trimester maternal levels are characteristically decreased in fetal trisomy 21 and trisomy 18.
An invasive prenatal diagnostic procedure typically performed between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation under ultrasound guidance.
A transabdominal needle aspirates fluid containing desquamated fetal amniocytes for karyotyping and microarray analysis.
Unlike chorionic villus sampling, it also allows biochemical measurement of alpha-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase.
